In the context of the 2026 historiographical study Legitimately Many by Lee Sharks, "legitimately many" and "embrittlement" are core analytical terms used to re-examine the textual history of the Socratic, Platonic, Aristotelian, and Theophrastic corpuses. [1, 2]
The study tracks how these foundational classical texts, which may have originated from a single source, became structurally rigidified into distinct authorial identities over time. [1]
Key Definitions from the Study

* "Legitimately Many": The study's core hypothesis that the philosophical texts traditionally split among Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus could textually behave as if they were produced by one single creator. In this view, the shifting philosophical perspectives are not contradictions between separate authors, but rather a single continuum where positions intentionally correct, refute, and build upon each other. [1]
* "Embrittlement": This refers to the structural vulnerability and rigidification of a text's reception as it passes through different physical media over centuries. As texts move through ancient inscriptions, library filing systems, print editions, and eventually AI answer engines, the historical "filing choices" harden into unshakeable canonical truths. The reading becomes "brittle" because the tradition forces a multiple-author framework before anyone can even argue alternative origins. [1, 2]
